name: Nora Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say is confidential, with no name attached. What is a normal shift for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the hospital transport bookings row at a contact centre. A patient rings because a car is late for dialysis or the address on the dispatch sheet is wrong, and I phone the driver while another agent stays with the patient. I have a two-year college diploma and am one of the best at keeping a difficult booking from becoming a missed appointment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters most in that work, and who is at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The patient needs an arrival time they can rely on, not a comforting voice saying the wrong thing. I have never used the AI helper; I work from the live dispatch sheet and the driver's call. My partner Helen teaches music lessons, our grown son pays his own rent, and my higher late-shift wage has helped us save about eleven months of expenses; there are several similar centres in reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the row that a quicker booking note is useful only after someone checks where the car really is. A patient can miss dialysis while our dashboard congratulates itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect patients will keep calling us, and the late rate should continue in this mild picture. Eleven months saved and several local employers give Helen and me room if an ordinary problem turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep confirming dispatch with the driver and recording any repeated wrong addresses. In the first year of AI Plateau I would take those examples to our joint staff meeting and ask with other leads for enough paid time to call the driver before closing a case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our wages, not complacent about a wrong car. A quiet software year does not excuse a missed appointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the screen was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the screen showed a car outside the clinic while the driver was still at the depot. I called him and told the patient the truth, even though it made the wait longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Helen's income change the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen's lesson income moves around, but my late rate and our reserve cover normal swings. Our son is starting his own household; we do not need to ask him for money.

I would ask with leads for **paid checking time** at the staff meeting.
think: I expect my **late wage** to continue in a mild change.
I see **eleven months saved** and several local jobs as a workable buffer.
do: Keep confirming **car locations** with drivers and recording repeated wrong addresses.
Bring **wrong-address examples** to a shared staff request for paid driver-check time.
feel: I feel **calm** about money while serious about patient errors.
S0.quote: A patient can miss dialysis while our dashboard congratulates itself.
fieldNote: She relies on **driver calls**, not AI summaries, to check a live booking.
Her **higher late wage** and eleven-month reserve support a calm financial response.

steps.text: Keep calling drivers to confirm hospital transport locations and log repeated wrong addresses
Join other leads at staff meeting to request paid driver-check time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues routine bookings may move to software, but the late car still needs a person with time to call. I would ask the union branch to demand a written paid human exceptions rota and publish the missed-appointment count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep the hard calls, yet a smaller team could lose evening shifts and my late premium. Helen's lesson money varies, and eleven months saved will not replace that higher weekly wage forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would bring three missed-transport reports to the branch meeting and ask other leads to seek written paid exception hours. In the first year routine bookings move, I would keep offered paid calls and compare the late rota with our normal weekly pay; if a premium is cut, I would check posted nearby transport desks before leaving only for a signed offer with comparable weekly wages and hours after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my own evening pay, though I can take the problem to others. A saved cushion is a voice in the meeting, not a permanent payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a missed trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count a case as missed when the patient cannot attend the appointment, even if the bot sent a message saying the trip was booked. That number should sit beside the claimed savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take daytime work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could take a daytime desk, but only after comparing the whole weekly wage, not the title. A signed offer must still cover our bills after the journey and Helen's quieter lesson months.

I would put **missed appointments** beside software savings.
think: I could lose the **late premium** even if hard calls remain.
I cannot replace my **higher weekly wage** indefinitely with savings or variable lessons.
do: Bring **three missed-trip reports** to the union; request written paid exception hours and publication of missed-appointment counts.
Keep **paid calls** while offered; after a premium cut, check posted roles and leave only on signed comparable after-travel weekly terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible premium cut despite strong savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch thinking AI by 2028 could plan and answer hospital transport bookings before most of us can adjust. Robots for hands-on driving arrive about 2031, but the desk faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my paid booking hours could end quickly, even though the difficult patients still need someone. Eleven months saved gives me time and there are other centres, but Helen and I need a wage that lasts beyond a search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would join a branch request for written notice dates and remaining paid exception shifts, and compare our full-week pay with a year of bills. If most booking hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid clinic reception work nearby; I would accept only a written full-week wage and hours that cover our bills after travel, keeping any transport calls still offered until a real offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed because most of my own late wage could go at speed. Eleven months saved buys me time to search if my late-shift wage goes, but it cannot replace that wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a clinic whether the receptionist handles real patients or simply checks people into a screen. I would not pay for a certificate with no paid vacancy attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your son help with travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son could show us a bus route, but he has a household of his own. I would ask whether he is free to help with a journey, not plan around him driving us every day.

I would ask the branch for **written notice dates** and paid exception shifts.
think: I expect **most booking hours** could end quickly.
I have **eleven months saved** for a search, not a lasting replacement wage.
do: Join a **branch notice request** and compare full-week pay with annual bills in 2026.

feel: I feel **alarmed** at the possible rapid loss of my late wage.
S2.quote: Eleven months saved buys me time to search if my late-shift wage goes, but it cannot replace that wage.
fieldNote: She holds **available paid calls** until a real clinic offer passes the weekly bill test.
Her son's **journey help** remains conditional on his actual availability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to demand an honest comparison of paid human hours and missed appointments. Thinking AI reaches booking decisions by 2031, while capable robots for driving arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep complex patient calls for a while, but the organisation may still cut the number of paid leads. I would not treat my eleven-month reserve as a reason to accept a worse rota without asking questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would work with the union branch to publish quarterly paid exception hours beside missed-appointment counts. I would keep the late calls while they are paid, and if my own hours fall in the first year after 2031, I would visit posted local patient-service desks to ask what the paid duties actually are before making an application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, though I have time to gather a public record. A patient does not become less late because the dashboard closed the ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What duties would you ask about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the patient-service desk can telephone a driver or only print another appointment slip. I need to know which person has authority to fix a missed car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I cannot choose an age and say I will have enough income then. Helen and I would check actual statements and bills before reducing either of our paid weeks.

I would explain **2031 booking AI** precedes 2034 driving robots.
think: I may retain **complex calls** while losing paid lead hours.
I cannot use **eleven months saved** as an excuse to accept a worse rota.
do: Work with the **union branch** to publish quarterly paid exception hours beside missed-appointment counts.

feel: I feel **anxious** about lead hours, with time to gather evidence.
S3.quote: A patient does not become less late because the dashboard closed the ticket.
fieldNote: She links **paid hours** to patient outcomes through a worker-led count.

steps.text: Publish quarterly paid exception hours and missed-appointment counts with union branch
Keep paid late patient calls while the transport rota offers them
If hours fall after 2031, inspect posted local patient desks and actual paid duties before applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team a decade of warning should buy us the chance to record patient outcomes and paid work side by side. Thinking AI reaches bookings by 2036; driving robots are a later issue around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer late shifts, but I cannot name an income that would replace the premium. Eleven months saved is a choice buffer, not a pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter Helen and I would gather actual income statements and total a year of rent, travel and other bills. I would keep the paid transport queue and ask the branch for yearly paid human-hours figures; after 2036 I would reduce late shifts only if verified income covered our bills and otherwise keep the paid work actually offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual desk change, but our wages and reserve are secure now. A long warning gives us a way to check figures without asking the children for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count Helen's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count Helen's quiet teaching months rather than multiply one busy term by four. We need a full year of real money before deciding whether I can stop late calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son can visit and disagree with the figures, and that is fine. His own rent and work are his to manage; I would not enter his wage as ours.

I would say **2036 booking AI** comes before 2039 driving robots.
think: I cannot name **replacement income** for late shifts at 68.
I see **eleven months saved** as a buffer, not a pension amount.
do: Gather **actual income statements** with Helen and total a full year of bills.
Keep **paid transport calls** and join yearly human-hours requests; reduce late shifts only if verified income covers bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later changes while current wages remain secure.
S4.quote: We need a full year of real money before deciding whether I can stop late calls.
fieldNote: Her **eleven-month reserve** supports choice without proving retirement income.

steps.text: Keep offered paid hospital transport calls while annual income is checked
Join union branch request for yearly paid human booking hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture. Most of the paid booking week could go before a patient-service vacancy opens, and I need a written human-hours plan and a real paid role.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who answers when a patient misses dialysis because the car was sent to the wrong door. A quick booking is no help if the patient never arrives.

headlineQuote: A quick booking is no help if the patient never arrives.
portrait: A **58-year-old** senior hospital-transport agent with a two-year college diploma and exceptional difficult-call skill.
She **never uses AI**, checking live dispatch with drivers herself.
Her **higher late wage**, eleven months saved and many local desks give her room to choose.
She makes **shared worker requests** for paid hours and missed-trip figures without assuming retirement income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most booking hours before a paid patient-service vacancy opens.
whatWouldHelp: A **written human-hours plan** and a real posted paid role would help.
